The '''Bloc Québécois'''{{efn|Pronounced {{IPAc-en|ˈ|b|l|ɒ|k|_|ˌ|k|ɛ|b|ə|ˈ|k|w|ɑː}} {{respell|BLOK|_|KEB|ə|KWAH}}; {{IPA|fr-CA|blɔk kebekwa|lang|small=no}}, {{lit|Québécois [Voting] Bloc}}.}} ('''BQ''' or '''Bloc''') is a [[list of federal political parties in Canada|federal political party in Canada]] devoted to [[Quebec nationalism|Quebecois nationalism]], [[social democracy]], and the promotion of [[Quebec sovereignty movement|Quebecois sovereignty]].<ref>{{cite news |location=Canada |work=The Globe and Mail |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-bloc-quebecois-could-change-name-as-sovereigntist-party-looks-to/ |title=Bloc Quebecois could change name as sovereigntist party looks to rebuild |archive-date=24 January 2022 |access-date=19 January 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220124111923/https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-bloc-quebecois-could-change-name-as-sovereigntist-party-looks-to/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The Bloc was formed in the early 1990s by [[Member of Parliament (Canada)|Members of Parliament]] (MPs) who defected from the federal [[Progressive Conservative Party of Canada|Progressive Conservative Party]] and [[Liberal Party of Canada|Liberal Party]] during the collapse of the [[Meech Lake Accord]]. Founder [[Lucien Bouchard]] had been a cabinet minister in the federal Progressive Conservative government of [[Brian Mulroney]].

The Bloc seeks to create the conditions necessary for the political secession of [[Quebec]] from Canada and campaigns exclusively within the province during federal elections. The party has been described as [[social democratic]]<ref>The BQ is described as social-democratic:
*{{cite book |author=Steven Staples |title=Missile Defence: Round One |url=https://archive.org/details/missiledefencero00stap |url-access=registration |date=3 October 2006 |publisher=[[James Lorimer & Company]] |isbn=978-1-55028-929-9 |page=[https://archive.org/details/missiledefencero00stap/page/160 160]}}
*{{cite book |author1=Geoffrey Evans |author2=[[Nan Dirk de Graaf]] |title=Political Choice Matters: Explaining the Strength of Class and Religious Cleavages in Cross-National Perspective |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bZhcx6hLOMMC&pg=PA167 |date=28 March 2013 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0-19-966399-6 |page=167}}
*{{cite book |author=Anne Westhues |title=Canadian Social Policy: Issues and Perspectives |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kxg3tp2c6V0C&pg=PA437 |publisher=Wilfrid Laurier University Press |date=20 September 2006 |page=437 |isbn=978-0-88920-504-8}}
*{{cite book |author1=John Loughlin |author2=John Kincaid |author3=Wilfried Swenden |title=Routledge Handbook of Regionalism and Federalism |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nT8YpGSGDcIC&pg=PA179 |date=18 July 2013 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-136-72762-7 |page=179}}
*{{cite book |last1=Dickerson |first1=M.O. |last2=Flanagan |first2=Thomas |last3=O'Neill |first3=Brenda |title=An Introduction to Government and Politics: A Conceptual Approach |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LZKSMxXKQ6EC&pg=PA120 |publisher=Cengage Learning |date=11 March 2009 |page=120 |isbn=978-0-17-650042-9}}
*{{cite book |author=Paul Orlowski |title=Teaching About Hegemony: Race, Class and Democracy in the 21st Century|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oexQKlYx_lUC&pg=PA123 |date=21 June 2011 |publisher=Springer|isbn=978-94-007-1418-2 |page=123}}
*{{cite book |author=William Cross|title=Political Parties |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3d9G8yUG-9QC&pg=PA84 |date=1 January 2011 |publisher=UBC Press|isbn=978-0-7748-4111-5 |page=84}}
*{{cite book |author1=Kevin Farnsworth |author2=Zoë M. Irving |title=Social Policy in Challenging Times: Economic Crisis and Welfare Systems |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WxZJ56-Tno0C&pg=PA247 |year=2011 |publisher=The Policy Press |isbn=978-1-84742-827-1 |page=247}}</ref> and [[Quebec sovereignty movement|separatist]] (or "[[sovereigntist]]").<ref name="Dyck2011">{{cite book |author=Rand Dyck |title=Canadian Politics: Concise |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BUOoN8e5Ps0C&pg=PA211 |date=8 March 2011|publisher=Cengage Learning |isbn=978-0-17-650343-7 |page=211}}</ref><ref name="EvansGraaf2013">{{cite book |author1=Geoffrey Evans |author2=Nan Dirk de Graaf |title=Political Choice Matters: Explaining the Strength of Class and Religious Cleavages in Cross-National Perspective |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bZhcx6hLOMMC&pg=PA167 |date=28 March 2013 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-966399-6 |page=167}}</ref> The Bloc supports the [[Canada and the Kyoto Protocol|Kyoto Protocol]],<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> [[Abortion in Canada|abortion rights]],<ref name=":2" /> [[LGBT rights in Canada|LGBTQ+ rights]],<ref name=":3" /> legalization of [[Euthanasia in Canada|assisted suicide]],<ref name=":4" /> abolition of the [[Senate of Canada|Canadian Senate]],<ref name=":5" /> [[Republicanism in Canada|abolition of the monarchy]],<ref name=":6" /> the Quebec [[Act respecting the laicity of the State|secularism law]],<ref name=":7" /> and supports exempting Quebec from the requirements of the ''[[Canadian Multiculturalism Act|Multiculturalism Act]].''<ref name=":8" />

From the [[1993 Canadian federal election|1993 federal election]] until 2011, the Bloc was the largest party in Quebec and either the second- or third-largest party in the [[House of Commons of Canada|House of Commons]] through seven straight federal elections. The [[2011 Canadian federal election|2011 election]] saw the party win just four seats and lose [[official party status]] after a wave of support for the [[New Democratic Party]]. By 2014, the party had been reduced to two seats because of resignations and expulsions.  In the [[2015 Canadian federal election|2015 election]], the Bloc won 10 seats, even though the party's leader [[Gilles Duceppe]] failed to win a seat. In the [[2019 Canadian federal election|2019 election]], the party won 32 seats, regaining official party status as a result. In the [[2021 Canadian federal election|2021 election]], their seat count remained the same as the 2019 election. In the [[2025 Canadian federal election|2025 election]], the party saw a decline in seat and vote share after increased support for the [[Liberal Party of Canada|Liberal Party]] under [[Mark Carney]]. Due to the 2019, 2021, and 2025 elections resulting in a series of [[Liberal Party of Canada|Liberal]] [[Minority governments in Canada|minority governments]], the Bloc shared the [[Balance of power (parliament)|balance of power]] with the [[New Democratic Party (Canada)|New Democratic Party]].

The Bloc has strong informal ties to the [[Parti Québécois]] (PQ, whose members are known as ''{{lang|fr|Péquistes}}''), a provincial party that advocates for the [[Quebec sovereignty movement|secession of Quebec]] from Canada and its independence; however, the two parties are not linked organizationally. As with its provincial counterpart, the Bloc Québécois has been supported by a wide range of voters in Quebec, from sections of [[labour movement|organized labour]] to more [[Conservatism in Canada|conservative]] rural voters.<ref>{{cite news|title=Boisclair gets emotional talking about homophobia |url=http://www.ctv.ca/CTVNews/Canada/20070304/que_vote_070304/ |access-date=30 December 2011 |publisher=[[CTV News]] |date=4 March 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120329062646/http://www.ctv.ca/CTVNews/Canada/20070304/que_vote_070304/ |archive-date=29 March 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Results suggest rift between urban, rural voters|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/results-suggest-rift-between-urban-rural-voters-1.621773|access-date=14 May 2013|publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]]|date=24 January 2006|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130806144455/http://www.cbc.ca/story/canadavotes2006/national/2006/01/24/urban-rural-060124.html|archive-date=6 August 2013}}</ref> Members and supporters are known in French as ''{{lang|fr|bloquistes}}'' ({{IPA|fr-CA|blɔkist|lang}}).

==History==

===Origins===
[[File:Lucien Bouchard 2009.png|thumb|Lucien Bouchard became founding leader of the Bloc Québécois in 1990.]]

The Bloc Québécois was formed in 1990 as an informal coalition of Progressive Conservative and Liberal Members of Parliament from Quebec, who left their original parties around the time of the defeat of the [[Meech Lake Accord]]. The party was intended to be temporary and was given the goal of the promotion of sovereignty at the federal level. The party aimed to disband following a successful [[referendum]] on secession from Canada. As with most parties, it has gained and lost prominent supporters over the years.<ref name="through the years" />

The initial coalition that led to the Bloc was headed by [[Lucien Bouchard]], who had been federal [[Minister of the Environment (Canada)|Minister of the Environment]] in the [[Progressive Conservative Party of Canada|Progressive Conservative]] government of [[Brian Mulroney]].<ref name="through the years">{{cite news|title=The Bloc Québécois through the years|url=http://m.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/the-bloc-qubcois-through-the-years/article2008919/?service=mobile|access-date=13 May 2011|newspaper=[[The Globe and Mail]]|date=3 May 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110508060618/http://m.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/the-bloc-qubcois-through-the-years/article2008919/?service=mobile|archive-date=8 May 2011}}</ref> Bouchard abandoned the government in May 1990 in response to the report of a commission headed by [[Jean Charest]] that suggested changes to the Meech Lake Accord. Bouchard felt the recommendations for change undermined the objectives and spirit of the accord. According to ''[[The Secret Mulroney Tapes]]'' he was fired by Prime Minister Mulroney. Bouchard was joined by five of his fellow Tories ([[Nic Leblanc]], [[Louis Plamondon]], [[Benoît Tremblay]], [[Gilbert Chartrand]], and [[François Gérin]]), along with two Liberals ([[Gilles Rocheleau]] and [[Jean Lapierre]]). The first Bloquiste candidate to be elected was [[Gilles Duceppe]], then a union organizer, in [[1990 Laurier—Sainte-Marie federal by-election|a by-election]] for the [[Montreal]] [[Electoral district (Canada)|riding]] of [[Laurier—Sainte-Marie]] on 13 August 1990.<ref name="through the years"/><ref>{{cite web|title=DUCEPPE, Gilles|url=http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ed3d4160-8a5a-4efc-a0a6-d65deeb994d9&Language=E&Section=FederalExperience|publisher=[[Parliament of Canada]]|access-date=13 May 2011|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120228190447/http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ed3d4160-8a5a-4efc-a0a6-d65deeb994d9&Language=E&Section=FederalExperience|archive-date=28 February 2012}}</ref> He ran as an independent, since the Bloc had not been registered as a federal party.

===First election and Official Opposition===
[[File:Bloc Quebecois 1990s.svg|thumb|300px|Logo of the Bloc Québécois in the 1990s to 2000s]]
In the [[1993 Canadian federal election|1993 federal election]], the Bloc won 54 seats (out of 75) in Quebec, sweeping nearly all of the francophone ridings. Because the opposition vote in the rest of Canada was split between the [[Reform Party of Canada|Reform Party]], the Progressive Conservative Party, and the [[New Democratic Party (Canada)|New Democratic Party]], the Bloc narrowly won the second largest number of seats in the House of Commons, and therefore became the [[Official Opposition (Canada)|official opposition]]. While Reform finished second in the national popular vote, the Bloc's heavy concentration of support in Quebec was slightly larger than Reform's concentration in the West.<ref>{{cite news|title=Bloc Québécois forms the Opposition in 1993 election|url=http://www.cbc.ca/player/Digital+Archives/Politics/Federal+Politics/ID/1632493560/?page=6|access-date=26 May 2013|newspaper=Canadian Broadcasting Corporation Digital Archives|date=26 October 1993|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150219092100/http://www.cbc.ca/player/Digital+Archives/Politics/Federal+Politics/ID/1632493560/?page=6|archive-date=19 February 2015}}</ref>

Soon after the 35th Parliament convened, Bouchard announced that Bloquiste MPs would only speak French on the floor of the House of Commons, a policy that remains in force to this day.  This was out of necessity; although Bouchard and most of the Bloc's founding members were fluently bilingual in French and English, Bouchard had discovered that most of his large caucus could not speak English well enough to use it in debate.

The election of such a relatively large number of Bloquistes was the first of [[The Three Periods]], a plan intended to lay out the way to sovereignty created by PQ leader [[Jacques Parizeau]]. Parizeau became [[Premier of Quebec]] in the [[1994 Quebec general election|Quebec election of 1994]] (the second of the ''Three Periods'').

Because the Bloc was the official opposition, it had considerable privileges over the other parties although all of its MPs had been elected in one province.  For instance, [[Question Period]]s during the 35th Parliament were dominated by issues of national unity.  However, the governing Liberals regarded Reform as their main opposition on non-Quebec matters.  Also, in 1995, when Bouchard garnered an invitation to meet visiting US President [[Bill Clinton]] by virtue of being Opposition Leader, Reform leader [[Preston Manning]] was also given a meeting with Clinton in order to defuse Bouchard's separatist leverage.<ref>{{cite web|author=Warren Caragata in Ottawa with Carl Mollins in Washington |url=http://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.com/index.cfm?PgNm=TCE&Params=M1ARTM0010399|title=Clinton visits Chrétien|date=6 March 1995|work=[[Maclean's]]|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090428054316/http://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.com/index.cfm?PgNm=TCE&Params=M1ARTM0010399|access-date=22 August 2019|archive-date = 28 April 2009}}</ref>

===1995 Quebec referendum and aftermath===
In 1995, the PQ government called the second [[1995 Quebec referendum|referendum]] on independence in [[History of Quebec|Quebec history]]. The Bloc entered the campaign for the ''Oui'' (Yes) side (in favour of sovereignty). The ''Oui'' side's campaign had a difficult beginning, so the leadership of the campaign was shifted from PQ leader Jacques Parizeau to Bloc leader Lucien Bouchard.  Bouchard was seen as more charismatic and more moderate, and therefore more likely to attract voters.<ref>{{cite news|title=The 1995 Quebec referendum: Turning the 'Yes' tide|url=http://www.cbc.ca/archives/categories/politics/federal-politics/separation-anxiety-the-1995-quebec-referendum/turning-the-yes-tide.html|access-date=14 May 2013|publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]]|date=30 October 1995|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130211091454/http://www.cbc.ca/archives/categories/politics/federal-politics/separation-anxiety-the-1995-quebec-referendum/turning-the-yes-tide.html|archive-date=11 February 2013}}</ref>

A "tripartite agreement" mapping out the plan for accession to independence was written and signed by the leaders of the Parti Québécois, the Bloc Québécois and the [[Action démocratique du Québec]] on 12 June 1995.<ref>{{cite news |title=1995 Quebec referendum: A "Yes" alliance |url=http://www.cbc.ca/archives/categories/politics/federal-politics/separation-anxiety-the-1995-quebec-referendum/a-common-front.html |access-date=14 May 2013 |publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]] |date=12 June 1995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130210231431/http://www.cbc.ca/archives/categories/politics/federal-politics/separation-anxiety-the-1995-quebec-referendum/a-common-front.html |archive-date=10 February 2013}}</ref> It revived [[René Lévesque]]'s notion that the referendum should be followed by the negotiating of an association agreement between an independent Quebec and the rest of Canada. This provision was inspired by Bouchard. Parizeau had previously wanted a vote simply on independence. The difference became moot when 50.6% of voters taking part in the referendum rejected the sovereignty plan. An overwhelming "Non" vote in Montreal tipped the balance.<ref>{{cite book |last=Cardinal |first=Mario |title=Breaking Point: Quebec, Canada, The 1995 Referendum |location=Montreal |publisher=Bayard Canada Books |isbn=2-89579-068-X |year=2005 |page=405}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=DGEQ October 30, 1995 Results |url=http://www.electionsquebec.qc.ca/francais/tableaux/referendum-1995-8481.php |website=Le Directeur général des élections du Québec |access-date=January 27, 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141213023157/http://www.electionsquebec.qc.ca/francais/tableaux/referendum-1995-8481.php |archive-date=December 13, 2014}}</ref>

The day after the referendum, Parizeau announced his pending resignation as PQ leader and [[Premier of Quebec]]. Bouchard left federal politics and succeeded Parizeau in both posts on 26 January 1996.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Pearlstein |first1=Steven |title=Separatists Win Quebec Elections |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/inatl/longterm/canada/stories/elections120198.htm |access-date=25 October 2022 |newspaper=Washington Post |agency=Washington Post Foreign Service |date=December 1, 1998 |archive-date=13 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220313025033/https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/inatl/longterm/canada/stories/elections120198.htm |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=May 1, 1998 |title=Charest takes Liberal reins: New leader heaps scorn on Quebec separatists |work=[[Calgary Herald]] |page=A4}}</ref><ref name="turner19970920">{{cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1997-sep-20-mn-34188-story.html |title=Provinces Brainstorm on Issue of Quebec Secession |last=Turner |first=Craig |date=1997-09-20 |work=Los Angeles Times |access-date=2019-07-08 |language=en-US |issn=0458-3035 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190708231735/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1997-sep-20-mn-34188-story.html |archive-date=2019-07-08 |url-status=live}}</ref> 

Following Bouchard's departure from Ottawa, [[Michel Gauthier]] became [[Bloc Québécois leadership elections|leader of the Bloc]]. In the wake of the referendum defeat, Gauthier proved unable to hold the fractious caucus together and resigned as leader just one year later. Gilles Duceppe, who had served as interim leader between Bouchard and Gauthier, became leader of the Bloc in 1997.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/duceppe-resigns-as-bloc-leader-after-losing-riding/article2007598/ | location=Toronto | work=The Globe and Mail | title=Duceppe resigns as Bloc leader after losing riding | date=24 August 2012 | url-status=live | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110505112408/http://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/duceppe-resigns-as-bloc-leader-after-losing-riding/article2007598/ | archive-date=5 May 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.thestar.com/news/canada/article/984484--duceppe-resigns-as-bloc-quebecois-drowns-in-an-orange-tsunami?bn=1 | location=Toronto | work=The Star | first=Andrew | last=Chung | title=Duceppe resigns as Bloc Québécois drowns in an orange tsunami | date=3 May 2011 | url-status=live | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121024031701/http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/article/984484--duceppe-resigns-as-bloc-quebecois-drowns-in-an-orange-tsunami?bn=1 | archive-date=24 October 2012}}</ref>

===Party under Gilles Duceppe===
[[File:Gilles Duceppe 2011-04-01 (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|Gilles Duceppe became the first Bloc MP in 1990; he served as leader from 1997 to 2011.]]

In the [[1997 Canadian federal election|1997 federal election]], the Bloc Québécois dropped to 44 seats, losing official opposition status to the Reform Party. The 1997–2000 term was marked by the Bloc's fight against the passage of the [[Clarity Act]], the attempt by Canadian Prime Minister [[Jean Chrétien]] (himself a Quebecer who represented a strongly nationalist riding) and [[Stéphane Dion]], a Quebec minister in Chrétien's cabinet, to codify the [[Supreme Court of Canada]]'s [[Reference Re Secession of Quebec|1998 decision]] that Quebec could not secede unilaterally.<ref>{{cite news|last=Dion|first=Stéphane|title=Stéphane Dion: Quebeckers want more clarity than 50% plus one|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/commentary/stphane-dion-quebeckers-want-more-clarity-than-50-plus-one/article8329073/|access-date=8 May 2013|newspaper=The Globe and Mail|date=7 February 2013}}</ref>

In the [[2000 Canadian federal election|2000 election]], the Bloc dropped further to 38 seats, despite polling a larger percentage of the vote than at the previous election. One factor was the [[2000–06 municipal reorganization in Quebec|forced merger of several major Quebec cities]], such as [[Montreal]], [[Quebec City]] and [[Hull, Quebec|Hull]]/[[Gatineau]]. The merger was very unpopular in those areas, resulting in Liberal wins in several of the merged areas. This was still more than the number of seats the Liberals had won in Quebec. However, the Liberals won several subsequent by-elections during the life of the 37th Parliament, until the Liberals had held the majority of Quebec's seats in the Commons for the first time since the [[1984 Canadian federal election|1984 federal election]]. From then to the subsequent election, the Bloc continued to denounce the federal government's interventions in what the Bloc saw as exclusively provincial jurisdictions. The Bloc credits its actions for the uncovering of what has since become the [[sponsorship scandal]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Federal sponsorship scandal|url=http://www.cbc.ca/news2/background/groupaction/|access-date=24 April 2014|publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]]|date=26 October 2006|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140515152950/http://www.cbc.ca/news2/background/groupaction/|archive-date=15 May 2014}}</ref>

The Bloc continued to slide in most of the 2003 opinion polls following the [[2003 Quebec general election|2003 Quebec election]] which was won by the federalist [[Quebec Liberal Party]] led by [[Jean Charest]]. However, things changed during the winter of 2003. The federalist Charest government lost popularity. Then, in February 2004, the Auditor General of Canada uncovered the [[Gomery Commission|sponsorship scandal]], suggesting illegality in the spending of federal monies in Quebec in support of Canadian unity. As well, the [[Liberal Party of Canada|Liberal]] government of [[Jean Chrétien]] passed party financing legislation that resulted in the Bloc receiving millions of dollars in subsidies that helped to stabilize its organization.<ref>{{cite news|title=Political contributions: money, money, money|url=http://www.cbc.ca/news2/background/cdngovernment/political-contributions.html|access-date=24 April 2014|publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]]|date=5 June 2006|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140401043433/http://www.cbc.ca/news2/background/cdngovernment/political-contributions.html|archive-date=1 April 2014}}</ref>

For the [[2004 Canadian federal election|2004 election]], the Bloc adopted the slogan ''Un parti propre au Québec'', a play on words that can be translated either as "A party of Quebec's own" ("a party proper to Quebec") or as "A clean party in Quebec". The Bloc won 54 seats in the House of Commons, tying its previous record from the 1993 campaign. For the [[2006 Canadian federal election|2006 election]], the Bloc used the slogan ''Heureusement, ici, c'est le Bloc!'' ("Fortunately, the Bloc is here!").<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bloc.org/archivage/depmontreal_english.pdf |title=BQ_DepEthno – anglais |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060219011054/http://www.bloc.org/archivage/depmontreal_english.pdf |archive-date=19 February 2006 }}</ref> The Bloc were expected to easily win more than 60 seats at the start of the campaign, and they did in fact take six seats from the Liberals. However, the unexpected surge of the new [[Conservative Party of Canada]] in parts of Quebec, particularly in and around Quebec City, led to the Bloc losing eight seats to the Tories. Coupled with an additional loss to [[André Arthur]], an independent candidate, the Bloc recorded a net loss of three seats.<ref>{{cite news|title=Conservatives make breakthrough in Quebec; Bloc wins 51 seats|url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/conservatives-make-breakthrough-in-quebec-bloc-wins-51-seats-1.586146|access-date=24 April 2014|publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]]|date=24 January 2006|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140416201625/http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/conservatives-make-breakthrough-in-quebec-bloc-wins-51-seats-1.586146|archive-date=16 April 2014}}</ref>

The Conservative Party won a plurality of seats in the House of Commons, thus forming a [[minority government]]. There was persistent speculation as to the possibility of the Bloc forming alliances with other opposition parties to wrest the government away from the Conservatives. Duceppe, whose leadership was confirmed after the election, maintained that the Bloc would continue to co-operate with other opposition parties or with the government when this advantaged Quebec, but would not participate in a federal government.{{Citation needed|date=March 2011}}

Gilles Duceppe announced on 11 May 2007 that he would run for the leadership of the Parti Québécois to replace [[André Boisclair]], who resigned on 8 May 2007, after the poor performance in the March 2007 [[2007 Quebec general election|Quebec provincial election]] and internal dissent forced him to step down. Duceppe announced the next day that he was withdrawing from the race, and that he would support [[Pauline Marois]] who had also announced her intention to run.<ref>{{cite news|title=Duceppe drops out of PQ race|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/duceppe-drops-out-of-pq-race-1.675571|access-date=8 May 2013|publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]]|date=12 May 2007|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130315002030/http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/story/2007/05/12/duceppe-pq.html|archive-date=15 March 2013}}</ref>

The Bloc made slight gains following the [[2008 Canadian federal election|2008 federal elections]] as they won 49 seats, one more than the number they had before the [[39th Canadian Parliament|previous parliament]] was dissolved. In that election, they used the slogan "''{{lang|fr|Présent pour le Québec}}''" ("Present for Quebec"). Although they made small gains in relation to the number of seats at dissolution, they fell by 2 seats to 49 in comparison to the 51 they received in 2006. Also, the proportion of popular votes in the province was down 4 points to 38.1%, the Bloc's lowest score since 1997.

In a speech in front of his supporters following the election, BQ leader Gilles Duceppe claimed to have achieved his objectives, adding: "without the Bloc Québécois tonight, Mr. Harper would have formed a majority government".<ref>{{cite news|title=Harper 'very pleased' with stronger minority|url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/harper-very-pleased-with-stronger-minority-1.707322|access-date=2 June 2018|publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]]|date=15 October 2008|archive-date=7 May 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180507202221/http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/harper-very-pleased-with-stronger-minority-1.707322|url-status=live}}</ref>

At the end of November 2008, the Bloc indicated that it would support a [[40th Canadian Parliament#Possible Motion of No Confidence|possible motion of no confidence]] against the governing Conservatives by the two other opposition parties, and would support the resulting Liberal-NDP coalition government at least until June 2010, without actually being part of the government.<ref>{{cite news|title=Liberals, NDP, Bloc sign deal on proposed coalition|url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/liberals-ndp-bloc-sign-deal-on-proposed-coalition-1.700119|access-date=2 June 2018|publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]]|date=1 December 2008|archive-date=28 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160228223101/http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/liberals-ndp-bloc-sign-deal-on-proposed-coalition-1.700119|url-status=live}}</ref>

====Coalition attempt====
On 26 March 2011, Bloc Québécois leader Duceppe stated that Conservative leader Stephen Harper had in 2004 tried to form a [[coalition government]] with the Bloc and NDP in response to Harper's allegations that the Liberals intended to form a coalition with the Bloc and the NDP.<ref>{{cite news|last=Payton|first=Laura|title=Harper wanted 2004 coalition: Duceppe|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/harper-wanted-2004-coalition-duceppe-1.1118390|access-date=26 March 2011|publisher=CBC News|date=26 March 2011|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111104222524/http://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/canadavotes2011/story/2011/03/26/cv-kickoff-bloc.html|archive-date=4 November 2011}}</ref> Two months after the 2004 federal election, Stephen Harper privately met with BQ leader Gilles Duceppe and New Democratic Party leader [[Jack Layton]] in a Montreal hotel.<ref name=gazetteCoalition/> On 9 September 2004, the three signed a letter addressed to then-[[Governor General of Canada|Governor General]] [[Adrienne Clarkson]], stating:
{{Blockquote|We respectfully point out that the opposition parties, who together constitute a majority in the House, have been in close consultation. We believe that, should a request for dissolution arise, this should give you cause, as constitutional practice has determined, to consult the opposition leaders and consider all of your options before exercising your constitutional authority.<ref name=gazetteCoalition>{{cite news|title=Harper, Layton, Duceppe sought 'co-opposition' in 2004 letter to GG |url=http://www.canada.com/news/Harper+Layton+Duceppe+sought+opposition+2004+letter/4511865/story.html |newspaper=[[The Gazette (Montreal)]] |date=27 March 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110401200203/http://www.canada.com/news/Harper%2BLayton%2BDuceppe%2Bsought%2Bopposition%2B2004%2Bletter/4511865/story.html |archive-date= 1 April 2011 }}</ref>}}

On the same day the letter was written, the three party leaders held a joint press conference at which they expressed their intent to co-operate on changing parliamentary rules, and to request that the governor general consult with them before deciding to call an election.<ref name=Harpercoalition>{{cite news|last=Chung|first=Andrew|title=Bloc leader accuses Harper of lying about coalition|url=https://www.thestar.com/news/canada/politics/article/962240--bloc-leader-accuses-harper-of-lying-about-coalition?bn=1|access-date=27 March 2011|newspaper=[[Toronto Star]]|date=26 March 2011|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121023204043/http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/politics/article/962240--bloc-leader-accuses-harper-of-lying-about-coalition?bn=1|archive-date=23 October 2012}}</ref> At the news conference, Harper said: "It is the Parliament that's supposed to run the country, not just the largest party and the single leader of that party. That's a criticism I've had and that we've had and that most Canadians have had for a long, long time now so this is an opportunity to start to change that." However, at the time, Harper and the two other opposition leaders denied trying to form a coalition government, despite the letter written to the governor general.<ref name=gazetteCoalition/> Harper said, "This is not a coalition, but this is a co-operative effort."<ref name=Harpercoalition/>

One month later, on 4 October 2004, journalist [[Mike Duffy]] (later appointed as a Conservative senator by Harper in December 2008) said "It is possible that you could change prime minister without having an election", and that some Conservatives wanted Harper as prime minister. The next day, Layton walked out on talks with Harper and Duceppe, accusing them of trying to replace [[Paul Martin]] with Harper as prime minister. Both Bloc and Conservative officials denied Layton's accusations.<ref name=gazetteCoalition/>

===Loss of official party status===
In the [[2011 Canadian federal election|2011 federal election]], in the wake of a surge of support for the New Democratic Party, the Bloc received less than a quarter of the popular vote in Quebec (and less than 6% of the national vote). It lost 44 of the 47 seats it held at parliament's dissolution, and only added one seat, which had been vacated by a Bloc Québécois member six months prior to the election. The seats lost included that of Duceppe, who resigned as party president and leader. It also lost all but one of its seats in Montreal.

By winning only four seats, the Bloc failed to reach the minimum of 12 seats required for [[official party status]] in the House of Commons.  MPs without official party status are treated as independents and must sit in the back row of the opposition benches. They are permitted just a few questions each week in question period and cannot sit as voting members on parliamentary committees.<ref>{{cite news|title=Duceppe quits after BQ crushed in Quebec|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/duceppe-quits-after-bq-crushed-in-quebec-1.1080086|access-date=7 May 2013|publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]]|date=2 May 2011|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130520213346/http://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/canadavotes2011/story/2011/05/02/cv-election-bloc-wrap-652.html|archive-date=20 May 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Bloc to seek party status, new leader: MP|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/bloc-to-seek-party-status-new-leader-mp-1.1117297|access-date=26 May 2013|publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]]|date=10 May 2011|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110808161017/http://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/story/2011/05/10/bloc-party-status.html|archive-date=8 August 2011}}</ref>

Elected to Parliament in this election were incumbents [[Louis Plamondon]], [[André Bellavance]], [[Maria Mourani]] and rookie MP [[Jean-François Fortin (politician)|Jean-François Fortin]]. When the 41st Parliament convened on 2 June 2011, Plamondon became the Bloc's interim parliamentary leader.<ref>{{cite web|title=Louis Plamondon nommé chef parlementaire par intérim du Bloc Québécois |url=http://www.blocquebecois.org/bloc.aspx?bloc=b9ce5ece-2021-43c3-a58b-bea951e2c974 |publisher=Bloc Quebecois |access-date=23 August 2011 |date=2 June 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110829173021/http://www.blocquebecois.org/Bloc.aspx?bloc=b9ce5ece-2021-43c3-a58b-bea951e2c974 |archive-date=29 August 2011 }}</ref> [[Vivian Barbot]] served as interim leader and party president following Duceppe's resignation until the party's 2011 leadership election.<ref name="BlocLeadership">{{cite web|title=LEADERSHIP ROLES|url=http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Party.aspx?Item=a639384e-e1a0-4169-83da-904925139b6a&Language=E|publisher=[[Parliament of Canada]]|access-date=28 May 2013|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130528182721/http://www.parl.gc.ca/ParlInfo/Files/Party.aspx?Item=a639384e-e1a0-4169-83da-904925139b6a&Language=E|archive-date=28 May 2013}}</ref>

The [[2011 Bloc Québécois leadership election|Bloc Québécois leadership election campaign]] to choose a permanent successor to Duceppe began on 17 September 2011. The campaign concluded on 11 December,<ref>{{cite web |title=La course à la présidence du Bloc Québécois aura lieu du 18 septembre au 11 décembre 2011 |url=http://www.blocquebecois.org/bloc.aspx?bloc=414b61d6-dccb-4398-8908-459a768bce22 |publisher=Bloc Quebecois |access-date=23 August 2011 |date=13 June 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110808114639/http://www.blocquebecois.org/Bloc.aspx?bloc=414b61d6-dccb-4398-8908-459a768bce22 |archive-date=8 August 2011 }}</ref> with the election of former MP for [[Hochelaga (electoral district)|Hochelaga]] [[Daniel Paillé]] as party leader.<ref>{{cite news |title=Daniel Paille elected Bloc Quebecois leader |url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/Daniel+Paille+elected+Bloc+Quebecois+leader/5844249/story.html |access-date=11 December 2011 |newspaper=The Gazette |location=Montreal |date=11 December 2011}}{{Dead link|date=July 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=11 December 2011 |title=Daniel Paille new leader of Bloc Quebecois |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/daniel-paill%C3%A9-new-leader-of-bloc-qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois-1.1073544 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240917202112/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/daniel-paill%C3%A9-new-leader-of-bloc-qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois-1.1073544 |archive-date=17 September 2024 |access-date=2025-05-04 |work=[[CBC News]]}}</ref> Plamondon, the longest-serving member of the Commons, served as parliamentary leader during Paillé's tenure as he did not have a seat.

On 28 February 2013, [[Claude Patry]] defected from the [[New Democratic Party (Canada)|New Democratic Party]] and joined the Bloc, citing his disagreement with the New Democratic Party on the subject of Quebec sovereignty, bringing the party's total seats in Parliament up to five.<ref>{{cite news|title=Mulcair calls on Patry to resign seat after defection to Bloc|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/mulcair-calls-on-patry-to-resign-seat-after-defection-to-bloc-1.1303285|access-date=7 May 2013|publisher=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]]|date=28 February 2013|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130509123328/http://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/story/2013/02/28/pol-mp-claude-patry-ndp-bloc-quebec-switch.html|archive-date=9 May 2013}}</ref>

The caucus fell back to four MPs on 12 September 2013 when Mourani, the party's only remaining member from Montreal, was expelled for her comments criticizing the [[Parti Québécois]] government's proposed Charter of Quebec Values.<ref>{{cite news|title=Bloc kicks out MP who spoke against Quebec religious-symbols ban|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/bloc-kicks-out-mp-who-spoke-against-quebec-religious-symbols-ban/article14273942/|access-date=12 September 2013|newspaper=The Globe and Mail|date=12 September 2013|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130912164623/http://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/bloc-kicks-out-mp-who-spoke-against-quebec-religious-symbols-ban/article14273942/|archive-date=12 September 2013}}</ref>

Paillé stepped down as leader on 16 December 2013 because of health reasons.<ref name="CBC News">{{cite news |url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/daniel-paill%C3%A9-leader-of-bloc-qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois-to-resign-1.2465588 |title=Daniel Paillé, leader of Bloc Québécois, to resign |date=16 December 2013 |access-date=16 December 2013 |publisher=[[CBC News]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180428015222/http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/daniel-paill%C3%A9-leader-of-bloc-qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois-to-resign-1.2465588 |archive-date=28 April 2018}}</ref> A [[2014 Bloc Québécois leadership election|leadership election]] was held the following June.<ref>{{cite news |title=Bloc Quebecois to pick new leader in May to replace Daniel Paille |url=https://montrealgazette.com/health/Bloc+Quebecois+pick+leader+replace+Daniel+Paille/9376769/story.html |access-date=15 January 2014 |newspaper=The Gazette |date=12 January 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140114175120/http://www.montrealgazette.com/health/Bloc+Quebecois+pick+leader+replace+Daniel+Paille/9376769/story.html |archive-date=14 January 2014}}</ref>

Hardliner [[Mario Beaulieu (politician)|Mario Beaulieu]], a former president of the [[Société Saint-Jean-Baptiste]] who had never been a Member of Parliament nor a member of [[National Assembly of Quebec|Quebec's National Assembly]], was elected party leader after running on a platform of prioritizing Quebec independence above all else. He defeated BQ Member of Parliament [[André Bellavance]], who had campaigned on a platform of broadening the Bloc beyond being a coalition of sovereigntists and had been endorsed by the rest of the party's caucus.<ref name=gaz>{{cite news |title=Bloc Québécois leadership candidate Mario Beaulieu wants to put sovereignty back on the front burner |url=https://montrealgazette.com/a9cois+leadership+candidate+Mario+Beaulieu+wants+sovereignty+back+front+burner/9791663/story.html |access-date=3 May 2014 |newspaper=The Gazette|location=Montreal |date=30 April 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140503003902/http://www.montrealgazette.com/a9cois%2Bleadership%2Bcandidate%2BMario%2BBeaulieu%2Bwants%2Bsovereignty%2Bback%2Bfront%2Bburner/9791663/story.html |archive-date=3 May 2014}}</ref>

On 12 August 2014, the caucus was reduced to three MPs when the Bloc's interim parliamentary leader, [[Jean-François Fortin (politician)|Jean-François Fortin]], quit the party to sit as an independent saying that the Bloc Québécois he had joined no longer existed and that Beaulieu had destroyed its credibility.<ref>{{cite news |title=Jean-Francois Fortin quits Bloc, says party no longer exists under new leader |url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/jean-francois-fortin-quits-bloc-says-party-no-longer-exists-under-new-leader-1.2734098?cmp=rss |access-date=12 August 2014 |publisher=CBC News |date=12 August 2014 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180428015222/http://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/jean-francois-fortin-quits-bloc-says-party-no-longer-exists-under-new-leader-1.2734098?cmp=rss |archive-date=28 April 2018}}</ref> On 25 August 2014, former interim parliamentary leader and failed leadership contender [[André Bellavance]] also resigned, reducing the Bloc to two MPs – one of whom, [[Claude Patry]], had announced that he would not run for re-election.<ref>{{cite news |title=Another Bloc MP quits party, leaving only two in Parliament |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/bloc-quebecois-mp-quits-party-pq-left-with-just-two-sitting-mps/article20191190/ |access-date=25 August 2014 |work=The Globe and Mail |date=25 August 2014 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140825225459/http://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/bloc-quebecois-mp-quits-party-pq-left-with-just-two-sitting-mps/article20191190/ |archive-date=25 August 2014}}</ref> On 31 December 2014, the party's vice president, Annie Lessard, resigned after a personality conflict with leader Mario Beaulieu.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/montreal/article/bloc-quebecois-vp-annie-lessard-resigns/ |title=Bloc Quebecois VP Annie Lessard resigns |publisher=CTV Montreal News |date=31 December 2014 |access-date=25 April 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170426152752/http://montreal.ctvnews.ca/bloc-quebecois-vp-annie-lessard-resigns-1.2167945 |archive-date=26 April 2017}}</ref>

====Return and departure of Duceppe====
With two seats left in parliament, and with the party languishing in the polls a few months before an expected election campaign, it was announced 10 June 2015 that Gilles Duceppe would be returning to lead the party into the campaign; Beaulieu would relinquish the leadership but remain party president.<ref name=back>{{cite news|title=illes Duceppe returns to lead Bloc Quebecois|url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/politics/gilles-duceppe-returns-to-lead-bloc-quebecois-1.2415002?hootPostID=062f4530d523c353466cfe09a9478b52|access-date=10 June 2015|work=CTV News|date=10 June 2015|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150610222826/http://www.ctvnews.ca/politics/gilles-duceppe-returns-to-lead-bloc-quebecois-1.2415002?hootPostID=062f4530d523c353466cfe09a9478b52|archive-date=10 June 2015}}</ref> The party executive agreed on 9 June 2015, to split the positions of president and party leader in order to facilitate Duceppe's return. The changes were approved by the party's general council on 1 July.<ref name=rat>{{cite news |url=http://www.cbc.ca/m/news/canada/montreal/gilles-duceppe-officially-named-leader-of-bloc-qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois-1.3135046 |title=Gilles Duceppe officially named leader of Bloc Québécois |publisher=CBC News |date=1 July 2015 |access-date=25 April 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924144719/http://www.cbc.ca/m/news/canada/montreal/gilles-duceppe-officially-named-leader-of-bloc-qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois-1.3135046 |archive-date=24 September 2015}}</ref><ref name=rat2>{{cite news|title=Returning Bloc leader Gilles Duceppe targets NDP for fall election|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/gilles-duceppe-returns-to-lead-bloc-quebecois/article24893180/|access-date=10 June 2015|work=The Globe and Mail|date=10 June 2015|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151121071123/http://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/gilles-duceppe-returns-to-lead-bloc-quebecois/article24893180/|archive-date=21 November 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Gilles Duceppe preparing comeback as leader of Bloc Québécois|access-date=4 May 2025|date=9 June 2015 |work=CBC News|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/gilles-duceppe-preparing-comeback-as-leader-of-bloc-qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois-1.3105751}}</ref>

[[File:Canadian federal election, 2015 results by riding - Bloc Quebecois strength.svg|thumb|Results of the [[2015 Canadian federal election]] showing support for Bloc Québécois candidates by riding]]
During the [[2015 Canadian federal election|2015 federal election]], the Bloc Québécois had hoped to pick up seats from the collapsing NDP vote; however, most Quebecers instead switched their allegiance to the Liberals and Conservatives rather than back to the Bloc. While the Bloc managed to win 10 seats, more than twice that of the previous election, it was not enough to gain official party status. The party's share of the popular vote in Quebec fell to 19%, its lowest point up until that time. As in 2011, Duceppe failed to win his own seat, and resigned again as party leader.<ref>{{cite news |author=Canada |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/former-pq-interim-leader-stephane-bedard-leaving-politics/article26925216/ |title=Bloc leader Duceppe, former PQ interim leader both resign |newspaper=The Globe and Mail |date=22 October 2015 |access-date=25 April 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170404163311/http://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/former-pq-interim-leader-stephane-bedard-leaving-politics/article26925216/ |archive-date=4 April 2017}}</ref>

===Party under Martine Ouellet (2017–2018)===
The party was led on an interim basis by [[Rhéal Fortin]] until the [[2017 Bloc Québécois leadership election|Bloc Québécois leadership election in March 2017]] acclaimed [[Martine Ouellet]], a member of the provincial [[National Assembly of Quebec]], as party leader.<ref name=bloc_leadership>{{cite web|url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/bloc-quebecois-leadership-who-is-martine-ouellet|title=Bloc Québécois' new leader: Who is Martine Ouellet?|work=The Gazette|location=Montreal|access-date=14 March 2017|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170314202301/http://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/bloc-quebecois-leadership-who-is-martine-ouellet|archive-date=14 March 2017}}</ref> Ouellet is not a Member of Parliament and intended to see out her term in the provincial legislature until the next provincial election in October 2018.

On 28 February 2018, seven of the Bloc's ten MPs quit the party's caucus to form the Groupe parlementaire québécois (later called ''[[Québec debout]]'') citing conflicts with Ouellet's leadership style and her insistence that the Bloc should emphasize promoting Quebec independence over "defending Quebec's interests".<ref>{{cite news|title=Bloc Québécois fractures as seven of 10 MPs quit over Ouellet's leadership|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/seven-of-10-bloc-quebecois-mps-quit-over-martine-ouellets-leadership/article38144355/#c-image-0|access-date=1 March 2018|work=The Globe and Mail|date=1 March 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180228200806/https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/seven-of-10-bloc-quebecois-mps-quit-over-martine-ouellets-leadership/article38144355/#c-image-0|archive-date=28 February 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Allard|first1=Clement|title=Seven of 10 Bloc Quebecois MPs quit over Martine Ouellet's leadership|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/seven-of-10-bloc-quebecois-mps-quit-over-martine-ouellets-leadership/article38144355/|access-date=28 February 2018|work=The Globe and Mail|agency=The Canadian Press|date=28 February 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180228180649/https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/seven-of-10-bloc-quebecois-mps-quit-over-martine-ouellets-leadership/article38144355/|archive-date=28 February 2018}}</ref> Three MPs remained in the Bloc's caucus: [[Mario Beaulieu (politician)|Mario Beaulieu]] ([[La Pointe-de-l'Île]]), [[Xavier Barsalou-Duval]] ([[Pierre-Boucher—Les Patriotes—Verchères]]), and [[Marilène Gill]] ([[Manicouagan (electoral district)|Manicouagan]]).

More than 20 ex-Bloc MPs, including [[Gilles Duceppe]], issued an [[open letter]] supporting the seven current MPs who had resigned from caucus and demanding Ouellet's resignation.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/more-than-20-ex-bloc-quebecois-mps-call-on-martine-ouellet-to-quit|title=More than 20 ex-Bloc Québécois MPs call on Martine Ouellet to quit|date=3 March 2018|website=The Gazette|location=Montreal|access-date=28 April 2018|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180304231538/http://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/more-than-20-ex-bloc-quebecois-mps-call-on-martine-ouellet-to-quit|archive-date=4 March 2018}}</ref> Nevertheless, after a lengthy meeting, the party's executive issued a statement supporting Ouellet's leadership but also stating that the seven rebels could keep their Bloc Québécois memberships and would not be expelled from the party for quitting the caucus, inviting them to return to the caucus in the future.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://montrealgazette.com/pmn/news-pmn/canada-news-pmn/bloc-quebecois-meets-to-discuss-fate-of-seven-mps-who-quit-over-leaders-style/wcm/771dd787-4bbd-4f05-86db-0d61b4af77bb|title=Bloc Québécois national office rallies behind Martine Ouellet|date=3 March 2018|website=The Gazette|location=Montreal|access-date=28 April 2018|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180304070939/http://montrealgazette.com/pmn/news-pmn/canada-news-pmn/bloc-quebecois-meets-to-discuss-fate-of-seven-mps-who-quit-over-leaders-style/wcm/771dd787-4bbd-4f05-86db-0d61b4af77bb|archive-date=4 March 2018}}</ref> A [[Léger Marketing]] poll conducted shortly after put the Bloc Quebecois at 12% among Quebec voters, its lowest rating ever. Following an election this would likely translate into zero seats, putting the survival of the party into question for the [[43rd Canadian federal election|2019 federal election]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Martine Ouellet won't surrender Bloc leadership, despite outcry by former MPs|url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/montreal/article/bloc-leadership-meets-to-discuss-referendum-question/|access-date=10 March 2018|work=CTV News Montreal|agency=The Canadian Press|date=10 March 2018|language=en-CA|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180310181148/https://montreal.ctvnews.ca/bloc-leadership-meets-to-discuss-referendum-question-1.3837327|archive-date=10 March 2018}}</ref>

A [[leadership review]] referendum was held on Ouellet's leadership on 1 and 2 June 2018<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/martine-ouellet-bloc-quebecois-leadership-referendum-1.4593688 |title=Referendum on Martine Ouellet's Bloc Québécois leadership set for 1–2 June |publisher=CBC News |date=26 March 2018 |access-date=10 June 2018 |archive-date=4 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180604210244/http://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/martine-ouellet-bloc-quebecois-leadership-referendum-1.4593688 |url-status=live }}</ref> resulting in the party membership rejecting her leadership by 67%, while a proposal that the party prioritize Quebec independence on a daily basis above all other issues also passed with 65% support. Ouellet subsequently announced her resignation as party leader effective 11 June 2018.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-martine-ouellet-loses-bloc-quebecois-leadership-confidence-vote/|title=Martine Ouellet loses Bloc Québécois leadership confidence vote|date=3 June 2018|website=www.theglobeandmail.com|archive-date=4 June 2018|access-date=4 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180604105825/https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-martine-ouellet-loses-bloc-quebecois-leadership-confidence-vote/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/martine-ouellet-steps-down-1.4690336 |title=Embattled Bloc Québécois leader Martine Ouellet resigns |publisher=CBC News |date=4 June 2018 |access-date=10 June 2018 |archive-date=4 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180604210700/https://www.cbc.ca/amp/1.4690336 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Following the announcement of Ouellet's resignation, MPs [[Michel Boudrias]] and [[Simon Marcil]] announced they would rejoin the party,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/bloc-quebecois-mps-return-quebec-debout-1.4694137 |title=Two of seven MPs who quit the Bloc Quebecois returning to the party |publisher=CBC News |date=6 June 2018 |access-date=10 June 2018 |archive-date=7 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180607214035/http://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/bloc-quebecois-mps-return-quebec-debout-1.4694137 |url-status=live }}</ref> while party president and MP [[Mario Beaulieu]] was named Ouelett's successor on an interim basis until her successor could be chosen.<ref name=mariointerim>{{cite news|url=https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/federal-leaders-including-trudeau-and-scheer-in-quebec-ahead-of-byelection|title=Federal leaders including Trudeau and Scheer converge on Quebec before byelection|date=14 June 2018|work=National Post|access-date=17 June 2018|language=en-US}}{{Dead link|date=August 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> On 22 August 2018, as part of an agreement to reunite the party, Beaulieu ceded the party presidency to Yves Perron; on 17 September 2018, the remaining MPs who had defected from the Bloc rejoined the party and dissolved their breakaway group, ''Québec debout''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/national/renegade-mps-to-return-to-bloc-quebecois-caucus |title=Renegade MPS to return to Bloc Québécois caucus |access-date=18 September 2018 |archive-date=18 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180918133132/https://montrealgazette.com/news/national/renegade-mps-to-return-to-bloc-quebecois-caucus |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Party under Yves-François Blanchet (2019–present)===
As the only candidate to have entered the race by the 15 January 2019 deadline, former [[Parti Québécois]] cabinet minister [[Yves-François Blanchet]] was named leader on 17 January 2019.<ref name="BlanchetWins">{{cite web |title=Yves-François Blanchet becomes Bloc Québécois leader |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/yves-fran-ois-blanchet-new-bloc-leader-1.4981556 |publisher=CBC News |access-date=17 January 2019 |date=17 January 2019 |archive-date=14 November 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191114025331/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/yves-fran-ois-blanchet-new-bloc-leader-1.4981556 |url-status=live }}</ref> After Blanchet became leader the BQ saw its support increasing in Quebec during the [[2019 Canadian federal election|2019 federal election]], which some considered to have exceeded expectations.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://globalnews.ca/news/6052964/bloc-quebecois-popularity-maxime-bernier/ |title=Surge in Bloc Quebecois popularity 'a little bit surprising,' says Maxime Bernier |website=Global News |access-date=4 January 2020 |archive-date=25 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191225144143/https://globalnews.ca/news/6052964/bloc-quebecois-popularity-maxime-bernier/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://ici.radio-canada.ca/nouvelle/1355328/elections-resultats-quebec-province-bloc-quebecois-npd |title=« Nous revenons de loin » : la résurgence du Bloc québécois se confirme |website=Radio-Canada |date=22 October 2019 |language=fr |access-date=12 April 2022 |archive-date=22 November 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211122213006/https://ici.radio-canada.ca/nouvelle/1355328/elections-resultats-quebec-province-bloc-quebecois-npd |url-status=live }}</ref> The BQ increased its number of seats from 10 in 2015, to 32 seats in 2019, both overtaking the [[New Democratic Party|NDP]] to become the third largest party in Canada and regaining [[official party status]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/big-gains-for-the-bloc-qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois-but-what-did-it-sacrifice-in-the-process-1.5330056|title=Big gains for the Bloc Québécois, but what did it sacrifice in the process? Social Sharing|last=Montpetit|first=Jonathan|date=22 October 2019|publisher=CBC News|access-date=30 November 2019|archive-date=6 November 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191106164018/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/big-gains-for-the-bloc-qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois-but-what-did-it-sacrifice-in-the-process-1.5330056|url-status=live}}</ref>

In the [[2021 Canadian federal election]], the BQ led by Blanchet won 32 seats, unchanged from the prior election.<ref>{{cite news |last=Connolly |first=Amanda |title=Liberals projected to form minority government |url=https://globalnews.ca/news/8206478/canada-election-results-2021/ |access-date=September 20, 2021 |work=Global News |date=September 20, 2021 |archive-date=December 29, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211229212410/https://globalnews.ca/news/8206478/canada-election-result |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Tasker|first=John Paul|date=September 20, 2021|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/federal-general-election-results-2021-1.6182364|title=Canadians have re-elected a Liberal minority government|agency=CBC|access-date=September 21, 2021|archive-date=January 20, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220120075227/https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/federal-general-election-results-2021-1.6182364|url-status=live}}</ref>

The Bloc Québécois held a leadership confidence vote in May 2023. Blanchet won 97% of the vote.<ref>{{cite news |first=Erika |last=Morris |title=Blanchet maintains 97% support of Block Québécois members in vote of confidence |date=20 May 2023 |work=CBC News |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/bloc-quebecois-blanchet-vote-of-confidence-1.6850721 |archive-date=2 July 2023 |access-date=2 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230702110346/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/bloc-quebecois-blanchet-vote-of-confidence-1.6850721 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In September 2024, the BQ won a competitive [[List of federal by-elections in Canada|by-election]] in [[2024 LaSalle—Émard—Verdun federal by-election|LaSalle—Émard—Verdun]] in [[Montreal]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Major |first=Darren |date=September 10, 2024 |title=Upcoming federal byelections will put Singh and the NDP brand to the test – NDP looking to both hold a Winnipeg seat and pull another away from the Liberals in Montreal |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/ndp-byelections-test-singh-leadership-1.7317935 |website=CBC News |access-date=11 September 2024 |archive-date=11 September 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240911151244/https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/ndp-byelections-test-singh-leadership-1.7317935 |url-status=live }}</ref> In the [[2025 Canadian federal election]], the BQ led by Blanchet won 22 seats, a significant decrease from the prior election.

==Relationship with the Parti Québécois==
The [[Parti Québécois]] has close ties to the Bloc and shares its principal objective of independence for Quebec. The two parties have backed each other during election campaigns, and prominent members of each party often attend and speak at the other's public events. In addition, the majority of each party's membership holds membership in both parties. However, on an organizational level the parties are separate entities – the Bloc is not the federal wing of the Parti Québécois, nor the PQ the provincial wing of the Bloc.

Lucien Bouchard has been the leader of both parties. Michel Gauthier, once Bloc's leader, was a PQ member of the [[National Assembly of Quebec]] from 1981 until 1988. Former party leader Daniel Paillé was also a PQ member of the National Assembly of Quebec from 1994 to 1996, and a BQ member of Parliament from 2009 to 2011.

In June 2014, [[Mario Beaulieu (politician)|Mario Beaulieu]], a former PQ riding president and Bloc candidate, was elected leader of the Bloc Québécois. Notwithstanding his previous ties to both parties, Beaulieu has been critical of what he sees as a too timid approach to sovereignty by both the Bloc and PQ. Beaulieu's election as Bloc leader was more warmly received by the PQ's rival party, [[Option nationale]], than by the PQ.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Don|first1=Macpherson|title=Mario Beaulieu's victory shows the Bloc's irrelevance|url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/Macpherson+Mario+Beaulieu+victory+shows+Bloc+irrelevance/9944189/story.html|work=[[The Gazette (Montreal)|The Gazette]]|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714181254/http://www.montrealgazette.com/news/Macpherson+Mario+Beaulieu+victory+shows+Bloc+irrelevance/9944189/story.html|archive-date=14 July 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Les députés bloquistes lancent un appel au calme|url=http://quebec.huffingtonpost.ca/2014/06/17/bloc-quebecois-mario-beaulieu-appel-au-calme-des-deputes_n_5502216.html|access-date=3 July 2014|work=[[HuffPost]]|date=16 June 2014|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714144354/http://quebec.huffingtonpost.ca/2014/06/17/bloc-quebecois-mario-beaulieu-appel-au-calme-des-deputes_n_5502216.html|archive-date=14 July 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Gagnon|first1=Lysiane|title=Will the Bloc Self-Destruct?|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/globe-debate/will-the-bloc-self-destruct/article19215051/#dashboard/follows/|access-date=3 July 2014|work=[[The Globe and Mail]]|date=18 June 2014|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140622013719/http://www.theglobeandmail.com/globe-debate/will-the-bloc-self-destruct/article19215051/#dashboard/follows/|archive-date=22 June 2014}}</ref>

[[Martine Ouellet]] was a PQ MNA from 2010 until 2017 and ran twice for the PQ leadership. She continued to sit in the Quebec National Assembly, as an independent MNA, after she was elected Bloc leader.

In the [[2015 Canadian federal election|2015 election]], Parti Québécois leader [[Pierre Karl Péladeau]] officially endorsed the Bloc, despite earlier calling the party useless.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/montreal/article/peladeau-offers-tepid-support-for-bloc-quebecois-at-weekend-rally-for-leader/|title=Peladeau offers tepid support for Bloc Quebecois at weekend rally for leader|work=Montreal|date=24 May 2015 |access-date=14 October 2015|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150810200752/http://montreal.ctvnews.ca/peladeau-offers-tepid-support-for-bloc-quebecois-at-weekend-rally-for-leader-1.2388610|archive-date=10 August 2015}}</ref>
Several incumbent PQ MNAs including [[Bernard Drainville]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://twitter.com/BDrainvillePQ/status/654390732942409728 |title=Bernard Drainville on Twitter: "Av @PJT2072 candidat du #Bloc ds Marc-Aur-Fortin & ERobillard de @kinosdesign, concepteur d'affiches de films, Laval" |via=Twitter |date=14 October 2015 |access-date=25 April 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305145950/https://twitter.com/BDrainvillePQ/status/654390732942409728 |archive-date=5 March 2016}}</ref>{{Primary source inline|date=September 2020}} [[Stéphane Bergeron]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://twitter.com/sbergeron/status/654399539793653760 |title=Stéphane Bergeron on Twitter: "Rencontre de presse suivie d'une visite, plus tôt, au CFP des Patriotes, en cie de @PKP_Qc, @daveturcotte & @caaths." |via=Twitter |date=14 October 2015 |access-date=25 April 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305135122/https://twitter.com/sbergeron/status/654399539793653760 |archive-date=5 March 2016}}</ref>{{Primary source inline|date=September 2020}} [[Maka Kotto]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://twitter.com/Maka_Kotto/status/650128869471703041 |title=Maka Kotto on Twitter: "Qui est le mieux placé pour représenter nos intérêts à Ottawa?: Le BLOC! @GillesDuceppe Bravo! Tu as surpassé nos attentes." |via=Twitter |date=2 October 2015 |access-date=25 April 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305134537/https://twitter.com/Maka_Kotto/status/650128869471703041 |archive-date=5 March 2016}}</ref>{{Primary source inline|date=September 2020}} [[Dave Turcotte]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://twitter.com/daveturcotte/status/654002067749666817 |title=Dave Turcotte on Twitter: "Rassemblement avec Catherine Fournier du #BlocQc et pkp_qc #TournéePQ #polqc #fed2015" |via=Twitter |date=13 October 2015 |access-date=25 April 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307223127/https://twitter.com/daveturcotte/status/654002067749666817 |archive-date=7 March 2016}}</ref>{{Primary source inline|date=September 2020}} and [[Agnès Maltais]]<ref>{{cite web |author=Agnès Maltais |url=https://twitter.com/AgnesMaltais/status/653232306979774464 |title=Agnès Maltais on Twitter: "Hier, j'ai voté pour Charles Mordret du Bloc Québécois. J'ai apposé ma croix avec fierté à côté de son nom." |via=Twitter |access-date=25 April 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161001173002/https://twitter.com/agnesmaltais/status/653232306979774464 |archive-date=1 October 2016}}</ref>{{Primary source inline|date=September 2020}} also endorsed the Bloc and campaigned for local candidates.
